  "text": "On the last morning at the shop, Martin took down the clock while his daughter counted the remaining rolls of thread.

“That belongs to the landlord,” she said.

“The bracket does.”

He laid the clock face down on a square of felt. Behind it, the wallpaper was darker, a clean circle above the faded shelves.

For thirty-eight years he had repaired shoes beneath that clock. Now the machine was sold, the benches were bare, and someone had booked a van for noon.

His daughter found a pair of children’s sandals in a paper bag.

“Uncollected,” he said.

“They’re tiny.”

“People forget.”

She checked the ticket. The date was eleven years old.

Martin reached for the bag, then stopped to wind the clock. He turned the key carefully, listening between each turn.

“You could put a notice online,” she said.

“For sandals?”

“No. About closing.”

“They’ll see the window.”

At half past eleven, a woman came in carrying one boot. Martin had already packed his apron.

“Only the buckle,” she said, then noticed the empty shelves. “Oh.”

He held out his hand.

His daughter watched him search three boxes for the small pliers. The woman waited by the counter, still wearing the other boot.

When he finished, he waved away her purse.

Outside, the van reversed towards the kerb.

His daughter lifted the clock from the felt.

“Kitchen?” she asked.

He considered it.

“Too loud.”

“Hall, then.”

Martin put the sandals into the box marked HOME. She moved the kettle aside to make room, and he folded the empty apron over them."
